143.history: The fishing town twenty miles up the coast from Seann Skell sent Tòmas mac Uilleim to the red hall in the first year with the telling that the far land lay behind the mist and could be smelt on some mornings. After the sailing Seonag nic Dhùghaill climbed its headland at first light in LE 66 and kept it through the day, and household after household took a turn after her; the custom was called Faire a' Chinn, the headland watch, and Seonag kept her own turns for forty years. The watch lapsed long before the age was out, and the fishing thinned with the rest of the north-west, until perhaps a dozen boats still put out from its shore. In LE 1,794 its fishers found a worked timber cast up, longer than any tree of the island and fastened with nails no smith of Dia-thìr had forged. In the last years of the age a fisher of the town, Oighrig nic Eachainn, rested on her oars past where the rule of sight-of-land allowed, saw a hard dark line beyond the grey for a few breaths, and turned for home and told only her mother.
143.known_for: the headland watch, and the timber out of the mist

305.history: The north-west coast town was a quiet reeve's post until the sea-thieves of the small islands began boarding the coasters off its shore in the eighth century of the count. Its reeve Coinneach mac Nèill counted the going as carefully as he had counted grain, and in LE 789 reported half the houses empty, their thatch going to moss; the crown reckoned his town's dues by the households that stood. When the thieves put in twice in a moon within sight of his harbour he asked the crown for a force, and Eilidh Bhàn sent Iain mac Thormoid by sea; the town's own fishermen led the boats through the channel to Eilean dhubh, where the thieves' hulls were burned, one of the town's own sons, Aonghas mac Ruairidh, was killed on the strand, and Uilleam Ruadh was taken. Then the harvests failed one on the heels of the last. The reeve's wife Beathag nic Artair died in the hard winter of LE 819, the last households loaded their carts and went inland, and Coinneach, reeve eight-and-forty years, shut his door and took the coast road east. A reeve sent down the empty coast in LE 1,694 counted more berths than households between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr.
305.known_for: the sea-thieves, and the reeve who stayed until the last cart

113.history: Fishers of the north coast settled in the eighth century of the count at the ford where the coast road crosses a clear stream, and by LE 835 a market had grown up on their strand trading north-coast fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of that coast no longer carried their catch the longer road south to Inis mhòr, and the ford town became the market of the north coast.
113.known_for: the strand-market of the north coast

261.history: The village in the north took its name from the oak grove on the hill above it, and in the fifth year Alasdair Saor came up the north road to fell it for the keels of the fleet. Its keeper, Eilidh nic Ruairidh, made him choose each tree he would take and hear its name; he chose fifty-four and left one young oak, the Child. Eighty men of the roll felled the grove through the summer, the greatest tree, the Queen, taking two days to bring down, and the keel-timbers went forty-two miles south to the sea on sleds of oak shod with ash, six yoke to a sled, over a causeway built across the stream below the village. The grove never grew again. The village built a low wall of stones round the Child, and its old keeper sat beside it every evening until dark. In LE 109 the vein-house set down the coppice law of Doire fhionn, and the village lived thereafter by cutting coppice rather than oak, some of the fellowship's released journeymen among its cutters.
261.known_for: the oaks felled for the fleet, and the Child walled on the hill

17.history: The river town of the north built barges in the second century of the count to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm and west along the cold way of the north coast, and a boy of the town watching the first one loaded asked his father why it should not simply cross open water by the shorter way, and got a look and no answer. Pupils of Dùn thais founded a house of disputation here in LE 769, the question of the vein argued in the north for the first time. The great gale of LE 1,229 drove the sea up the river higher than anyone living had seen and heaped the strand with broken plank. As the roads improved the coasting trade went by cart, and in LE 1,634 the last barge that had worked the cold way was hauled above the tide-line and chocked level, kept rather than broken up, though few of the town's fathers could say any longer what the cold way had been the way from.
17.known_for: the grain barges of the cold way, and the last one kept on the strand

24.history: The harbour town on the north coast took the dawn rite of the Hawk in LE 239, when two of Gormshuil nic Artair's pupils, a brother and sister of a coastal household, carried it down from Cnoc bheag so that the fishing families need not walk two days inland for it; Gormshuil came down herself to judge whether the teaching had travelled whole. Its hawk-house took charge of the measured burning for the country between the coast and the hills, and was eight years old when Gormshuil died. Ùisdean mac Pàdraig came here to gather what her pupils remembered for the Book of the Hawk, marking every saying he had not heard from her own mouth.
24.known_for: the second house of the Hawk

132.history: The northern Seann Skell, on the bay the hawk-keepers call their own, is not the river port of the west. In the fifth century of the count it put up a wall around its streets for the first time, and the crown granted a market inside the new landward gate where the amber of that coast was sold beside whale-oil, honey and the wool of the northern moors; the amber-workers swore to sell no rough stone outside the walls, and one of them, Ailig an Òir, forfeited a season's gathering to his own guild for breaking the oath within the year. After the schism of the Hawk the priests of the Fed Hawk settled here, and under Beathag nic Sheumais built a following of four families into a school. From here in LE 919 she rode to Cathair dhearg to ask that the measured handful be raised by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast, and carried the refusal home in her own satchel; the house stood after exactly as it had before.
132.known_for: the amber market inside the gate, and the house of the Fed Hawk

37.history: The harbour town of the north coast lost its old harbour wall in one night in LE 259, in the storm its fishers call Am Fuath Mòr, and with it forty boats at their moorings and eighteen men and women who had gone down in the dark to save them. Its young reeve, Raghnall mac Nèill, thirty-four and four years in office, stood knee-deep hauling on a rope to bring in a boat with two children lashed inside, and afterward lost his count twice burying the dead in a single row on the headland. The town built its wall again higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the capital's masons, and the hooked wall stood through every storm of the age after.

20.history: The walled town above the sacred forest kept the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age, and in the third century of the count the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair taught there that the hawk of the rite was Mòd himself, and that the vein under Muileann dhearg was a hawk of his kind, to be fed the measured handful and never glutted past it. Her father Artair kept the mews before her; she first called the hawk down alone at three-and-thirty. Her watchers raised Taigh an t-Seabhaig below the mews block in LE 232, and after her death Ùisdean mac Pàdraig wrote her sayings as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig. By royal grant in LE 471 the sacred forest passed to the priests of Macha alone. At the council of the Hawk here in LE 889 a young priest asked whether Mòd would rather starve a grown flock than see his handful grown to meet it, and those who held he would not were named the Fed Hawk and asked to keep their teaching elsewhere. In the eleventh century the priest Tòmas mac Aonghais cleared the moss from the old obelisk above the town with wooden scrapers and found letters no table of the schools could read.
20.known_for: the house of the Hawk and the Book of the Hawk
